books.title: The Happy Prince, and Other Tales

questions.question: What did Mrs. Rabbit buy at the baker’s?
questions.expected: A loaf of brown bread and five currant buns.

evidence.quote:
She bought a loaf of brown bread and five
currant buns.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote directly states Mrs. Rabbit bought a loaf of brown bread and five currant buns.

questions.question: Who does Mrs. Rabbit mean by “your Father” in her warning, and what happened to him?
questions.expected: She means the rabbits’ father; he was put in a pie.

evidence.quote:
your Father had an accident there; he was put in a pie by Mrs.
McGregor.'

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote addresses the children as “my dears,” refers to “your Father,” and says he was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor.

questions.question: Put Peter’s first three food stops in order.
questions.expected: He ate lettuces and French beans, then radishes, and then went to look for parsley.

evidence.quote:
First he ate some lettuces and some French beans; and then he ate
some radishes;
And then, feeling rather sick, he went to look for some parsley.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes give the sequence: lettuces and French beans, radishes, then looking for parsley.

questions.question: What did Mr. McGregor call out while chasing Peter?
questions.expected: “Stop thief!”

evidence.quote:
calling out,
'Stop thief!'

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote attributes “Stop thief!” to Mr. McGregor while he chases Peter.

questions.question: Why did Peter get caught in the gooseberry net?
questions.expected: Its large buttons caught on the net as he ran.

evidence.quote:
run into a gooseberry net, and got caught by the large buttons on his
jacket.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says Peter ran into a gooseberry net and got caught by the large buttons on his jacket.

questions.question: How did Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cottontail’s choice differ from Peter’s?
questions.expected: They went down the lane to gather blackberries, while Peter went into Mr. McGregor’s garden and squeezed under the gate.

evidence.quote:
Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cottontail, who were good little bunnies, went
down the lane to gather blackberries:

But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor's
garden, and squeezed under the gate!

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes contrast the three rabbits gathering blackberries down the lane with Peter entering Mr. McGregor’s garden under the gate.

questions.question: What did the mouse carry, and where was she taking it?
questions.expected: She carried peas and beans to her family in the wood.

evidence.quote:
carrying
peas and beans to her family in the wood.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says the mouse carried peas and beans to her family in the wood.

questions.question: What did the sparrows urge Peter to do, and what did he do when Mr. McGregor came up with a sieve?
questions.expected: The sparrows implored Peter to exert himself. When Mr. McGregor came up with a sieve, Peter wriggled out, leaving his jacket behind.

evidence.quote:
Peter gave himself up for lost, and shed big tears; but his sobs were
overheard by some friendly sparrows, who flew to him in great
excitement, and implored him to exert himself.

Mr. McGregor came up with a sieve, which he intended to pop upon the
top of Peter; but Peter wriggled out just in time, leaving his jacket
behind him.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state that the sparrows urged Peter to exert himself and that, when Mr. McGregor came with a sieve, Peter wriggled out of his jacket.

questions.question: Across the chase and Peter’s later recovery, what happens to the clothes he loses?
questions.expected: He loses his shoes while fleeing, leaves his jacket in the net, and Mr. McGregor hangs the jacket and shoes as a scarecrow.

evidence.quote:
He lost one of his shoes among the cabbages, and the other shoe
amongst the potatoes.

Peter wriggled out just in time, leaving his jacket
behind him.

Mr. McGregor hung up the little jacket and the shoes for a scare-crow
to frighten the blackbirds.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state that Peter lost his shoes, left his jacket in the net, and Mr. McGregor hung up the jacket and shoes as a scarecrow.

questions.question: Why could Mr. McGregor not follow Peter through the window?
questions.expected: The window was too small for Mr. McGregor.

evidence.quote: The window was too small for Mr. McGregor

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote directly states the window was too small for Mr. McGregor.

questions.question: Who told Peter about cats, according to the story?
questions.expected: His cousin, little Benjamin Bunny.

evidence.quote:
he had heard about cats from his cousin,
little Benjamin Bunny.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote identifies Peter’s cousin, little Benjamin Bunny, as the source of what he had heard about cats.

questions.question: After seeing the gate beyond Mr. McGregor, what did Peter do?
questions.expected: He quietly got down from the wheelbarrow and ran along the walk behind the black-currant bushes.

evidence.quote:
Peter got down very quietly off the wheelbarrow; and started running
as fast as he could go, along a straight walk behind some
black-currant bushes.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote describes Peter quietly getting down from the wheelbarrow and running along the walk behind the black-currant bushes.

questions.question: What made Peter leave the white cat alone?
questions.expected: He thought it best to go away without speaking because he had heard about cats from Benjamin Bunny.

evidence.quote:
Peter thought it best to go away
without speaking to her;

he had heard about cats from his cousin,
little Benjamin Bunny.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes link Peter’s decision to leave without speaking to having heard about cats from his cousin Benjamin Bunny.

questions.question: What places did Mrs. Rabbit say the children could go, and which place did she warn them to avoid?
questions.expected: They could go into the fields or down the lane, but she warned them not to go into Mr. McGregor’s garden.

evidence.quote:
'Now my dears,' said old Mrs. Rabbit one morning, 'you may go into
the fields or down the lane, but don't go into Mr. McGregor's garden:

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote names the allowed places—the fields or the lane—and warns against entering Mr. McGregor’s garden.

questions.question: When Peter asked the mouse for the way to the gate, how did she respond? Later, where did he see the gate?
questions.expected: The mouse could not answer because she had a large pea in her mouth and only shook her head. Later, Peter saw the gate beyond Mr. McGregor while peeping from the wheelbarrow.

evidence.quote:
Peter asked her the way to
the gate, but she had such a large pea in her mouth that she could not
answer. She only shook her head at him.

The first thing he saw was Mr. McGregor hoeing onions. His back was
turned towards Peter, and beyond him was the gate!

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state that the mouse could not answer because of the pea and shook her head, and that Peter later saw the gate beyond Mr. McGregor from the wheelbarrow.

questions.question: What did Peter’s mother wonder about his clothes, and what had Peter lost for the second time in a fortnight?
questions.expected: She wondered what he had done with his clothes. He had lost a little jacket and pair of shoes for the second time in a fortnight.

evidence.quote:
His mother was busy
cooking; she wondered what he had done with his clothes.

It was the
second little jacket and pair of shoes that Peter had lost in a
fortnight!

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state that his mother wondered what he had done with his clothes and that he had lost a second little jacket and pair of shoes in a fortnight.

questions.question: How did Peter’s escape from the shed differ from his escape attempt at the garden wall door?
questions.expected: He escaped the shed through a window, but the wall door was locked and offered no gap underneath for him to squeeze through.

evidence.quote: Peter, who jumped out of a window

He found a door in a wall; but it was locked, and there was no room
for a fat little rabbit to squeeze underneath.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes say Peter jumped out of a window, while the wall door was locked and had no room underneath for him to squeeze through.

questions.question: What was the white cat watching, and what movement did the narrator describe?
questions.expected: She was staring at gold-fish; the tip of her tail twitched now and then.

evidence.quote:
A white cat was staring at some
gold-fish, she sat very, very still, but now and then the tip of her
tail twitched as if it were alive.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says the cat stared at gold-fish and that the tip of her tail twitched now and then.

questions.question: What happened to Peter that evening, and what remedy did his mother give him?
questions.expected: He was not very well; she put him to bed and gave him camomile tea.

evidence.quote: Peter was not very well during the evening.

His mother put him to bed, and made some camomile tea; and she gave a
dose of it to Peter!

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes say Peter was not very well that evening and that his mother put him to bed and gave him camomile tea.

questions.question: What were Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail having while Peter was put to bed?
questions.expected: Bread and milk and blackberries for supper.

evidence.quote:
But Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail had bread and milk and
blackberries for supper.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote directly states that Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail had bread and milk and blackberries for supper.

questions.question: What was tucked between the Velveteen Rabbit’s paws on Christmas morning?
questions.expected: A sprig of holly.

evidence.quote:
with a sprig of holly between his
paws

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote directly says a sprig of holly was between his paws.

questions.question: Which toy was the only one kind to the Velveteen Rabbit in the nursery?
questions.expected: The Skin Horse.

evidence.quote:
the only person who
was kind to him at all was the Skin Horse.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote identifies the Skin Horse as the only one kind to him.

questions.question: Who made the Skin Horse Real?
questions.expected: The Boy's Uncle.

evidence.quote: "The Boy's Uncle made me Real," he said.

evidenceReview.rationale: The Skin Horse directly says the Boy’s Uncle made him Real.

questions.question: What did Nana call the Velveteen Rabbit when she put him into the Boy’s arms?
questions.expected: “Your old Bunny.”

evidence.quote: "Here," she said, "take your old Bunny! He'll do to sleep with you!"

evidenceReview.rationale: Nana directly calls him “your old Bunny.”

questions.question: What does the Skin Horse say makes a toy Real?
questions.expected: A child’s long, genuine love makes it Real.

evidence.quote:
When a child loves you for a long, long time, not just
to play with, but REALLY loves you, then you become Real.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says a child’s long, genuine love makes a toy Real.

questions.question: Why did the Boy’s Rabbit end up sleeping with him that first night?
questions.expected: Nana could not find the china dog that usually slept with the Boy, so she gave him the Rabbit instead.

evidence.quote:
he couldn't find the china
dog that always slept with him.
"Here," she said, "take your old Bunny! He'll do to sleep with you!"

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes establish that the china dog was missing and Nana offered the Rabbit for the Boy to sleep with.

questions.question: Why did the wild rabbits conclude that the Velveteen Rabbit was not a rabbit like them?
questions.expected: He had no hind legs, and one of the wild rabbits said he did not smell right.

evidence.quote: "He hasn't got any hind legs!"
"He doesn't smell right!"

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes give both reasons: he appeared to lack hind legs and was said not to smell right.

questions.question: What did the doctor order for the books and toys the Boy had played with in bed?
questions.expected: They were to be burned.

evidence.quote:
and all the books and toys that the Boy had played with
in bed must be burnt.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says the books and toys the Boy played with in bed must be burnt.

questions.question: How did the Skin Horse explain that a toy becomes Real?
questions.expected: A child must love it for a long time, not just play with it.

evidence.quote:
When a child loves you for a long, long time, not just
to play with, but REALLY loves you, then you become Real.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says a child must love the toy for a long time, not merely play with it, for it to become Real.

questions.question: According to the Skin Horse, what happens to a toy’s appearance as it becomes Real, and why does that not matter?
questions.expected: It may become shabby, lose hair, and have its eyes or joints wear out; once Real, it cannot be ugly to people who understand.

evidence.quote:
Generally, by the time you are Real, most of your hair has been loved
off, and your eyes drop out and you get loose in the joints and very
shabby.

because once you are
Real you can't be ugly, except to people who don't understand.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes describe the toy’s worn appearance and explain that a Real toy cannot be ugly to people who understand.

questions.question: What season does the passage say it was when the Boy went to play in the wood?
questions.expected: Summer.

evidence.quote: That was a wonderful Summer!

evidenceReview.rationale: The passage explicitly calls it a wonderful Summer.

questions.question: Which happened first: the Rabbit slept in the Boy’s bed, or the Fairy changed him?
questions.expected: The Rabbit slept in the Boy’s bed before the Fairy changed him.

evidence.quote:
That night, and for many nights after, the Velveteen Rabbit slept in
the Boy's bed.

He did not know that when the Fairy kissed
him that last time she had changed him altogether.

evidenceReview.rationale: The cited bed passage precedes the cited Fairy passage describing how she changed him.

questions.question: What changes to the Rabbit’s body did he discover after the Fairy kissed him?
questions.expected: He had hind legs and brown fur, and his long whiskers brushed the grass.

evidence.quote: And he found that he actually had hind legs!

Instead of dingy
velveteen he had brown fur, soft and shiny, his ears twitched by
themselves, and his whiskers were so long that they brushed the grass.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state that he had hind legs, brown fur, and whiskers long enough to brush the grass.

questions.question: What connection did the story draw between the Boy’s love and the Rabbit becoming Real?
questions.expected: The Boy’s love made the Rabbit Real to him; the Fairy said he would now be Real to everyone.

evidence.quote:
"You were Real to the Boy," the Fairy said, "because he loved you. Now
you shall be Real to every one."

evidenceReview.rationale: The Fairy directly connects the Boy’s love with the Rabbit being Real to him, then says he will be Real to everyone.

questions.question: How did Nana’s actions help bring the Boy and Rabbit together at bedtime?
questions.expected: When Nana saw the cupboard door open, she took the Rabbit from the cupboard and put him into the Boy’s arms.

evidence.quote:
so she simply looked
about her, and seeing that the toy cupboard door stood open, she made
a swoop.

And she dragged the Rabbit out by one ear, and put him into the Boy's
arms.

evidenceReview.rationale: Together, the quotes say Nana saw the open cupboard, pulled the Rabbit out, and put him into the Boy’s arms.

questions.question: How did the Skin Horse’s story shape the Rabbit’s hopes and worries?
questions.expected: The Rabbit longed to become Real but felt sad at the thought of growing shabby and losing his eyes and whiskers.

evidence.quote:
He longed to become Real, to know
what it felt like;

the idea of growing shabby and losing his
eyes and whiskers was rather sad.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes support both the Rabbit’s longing to become Real and his sadness about growing shabby and losing his eyes and whiskers.

questions.question: What do the Rabbit’s conversation with the Skin Horse and the Fairy’s explanation together suggest about being Real?
questions.expected: A child’s love makes a toy Real to that child, and the Fairy says she takes loved, worn-out toys and turns them Real when children no longer need them.

evidence.quote:
When a child loves you for a long, long time, not just
to play with, but REALLY loves you, then you become Real.

When they are old and worn
out and the children don't need them any more, then I come and take
them away with me and turn them into Real.

evidenceReview.rationale: The Skin Horse says a child’s long love makes a toy Real; the Fairy says the Boy’s love made the Rabbit Real to him and describes turning loved, worn-out toys Real.

questions.question: Compare how the mechanical toys and the Skin Horse regarded themselves and other toys.
questions.expected: The mechanical toys looked down on others and pretended to be real; the Skin Horse knew they were only toys and would not become anything else.

evidence.quote:
The mechanical toys were very superior, and looked down
upon every one else; they were full of modern ideas, and pretended
they were real.

he knew that they
were only toys, and would never turn into anything else.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes support the mechanical toys’ superiority and pretense, and the Skin Horse’s view that those toys would not turn into anything else.

questions.question: How did the wild rabbits’ response to the Rabbit differ from the Boy’s response to his worn appearance?
questions.expected: The wild rabbits said he was not real, while the Boy continued to love him and always thought him beautiful.

evidence.quote:
"He isn't a rabbit at all! He
isn't real!"

Weeks passed, and the little Rabbit grew very old and shabby, but the
Boy loved him just as much.

To him he was always
beautiful

evidenceReview.rationale: The wild rabbits say he is not real, while the quotes say the Boy loved him just as much and always thought him beautiful.

questions.question: At the end, who does the Boy think the rabbit resembles, and who does the narrator reveal it to be?
questions.expected: The Boy thinks it looks like his lost Bunny; the narrator reveals it really is his own Bunny, returned to see him.

evidence.quote:
"Why, he looks just like my old Bunny that was lost when I had scarlet
fever!"

But he never knew that it really was his own Bunny, come back to look
at the child who had first helped him to be Real.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state both the Boy’s mistaken resemblance and the narrator’s revelation that it was his own Bunny.

questions.question: What gems were set in the Happy Prince’s eyes?
questions.expected: Two bright sapphires.

evidence.quote: he had two bright sapphires

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says the Prince had two bright sapphires for eyes.

questions.question: Why had the Swallow stayed behind after his companions left for Egypt?
questions.expected: He was in love with a Reed.

evidence.quote:
His friends had
gone away to Egypt six weeks before, but he had stayed behind, for he was
in love with the most beautiful Reed.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says he stayed behind because he was in love with the most beautiful Reed.

questions.question: What was the seamstress’s sick little boy asking for?
questions.expected: Oranges.

evidence.quote:
her little boy is lying
ill.  He has a fever, and is asking for oranges.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says the boy was asking for oranges.

questions.question: After the boy is described as asking for oranges, what does the passage say his mother has to give him?
questions.expected: Nothing but river water.

evidence.quote:
His mother has nothing
to give him but river water, so he is crying.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote directly says his mother had nothing to give him but river water.

questions.question: Who remarked on the Swallow’s winter appearance, and where was he?
questions.expected: The Professor of Ornithology, passing over the bridge.

evidence.quote:
“What a
remarkable phenomenon,” said the Professor of Ornithology as he was
passing over the bridge.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote names the Professor of Ornithology and says he was passing over the bridge.

questions.question: What change followed when the Swallow distributed the Prince’s gold among the poor?
questions.expected: The children became rosier, laughed and played, and said they had bread.

evidence.quote:
Leaf after leaf of the fine gold he
brought to the poor, and the children’s faces grew rosier, and they
laughed and played games in the street.
“We have bread now!” they cried.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state that the children grew rosier, laughed and played, and cried that they had bread.

questions.question: What does the Tree say the Nightingale must do to make a red rose?
questions.expected: Build it out of music by moonlight, stain it with her heart’s-blood, sing with her breast against a thorn all night, and let the thorn pierce her heart so her life-blood flows into the Tree.

evidence.quote:
you must build it out of music
by moonlight, and stain it with your own heart’s-blood.  You must sing to
me with your breast against a thorn.  All night long you must sing to me,
and the thorn must pierce your heart, and your life-blood must flow into
my veins, and become mine.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote states all the listed instructions for making the rose, including music by moonlight, singing against a thorn, and life-blood flowing into the Tree.

questions.question: How did the Student misread the Nightingale’s sacrifice after hearing her final song?
questions.expected: He judged her to be all style without sincerity and thought she would not sacrifice herself for others.

evidence.quote:
she is all style, without
any sincerity.
She would not sacrifice herself for others.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes explicitly say the Student judged her insincere and thought she would not sacrifice herself for others.

questions.question: What two reasons did the Professor’s daughter give for refusing the Student’s rose?
questions.expected: She said it did not go with her dress and that the Chamberlain’s nephew had sent her real jewels.

evidence.quote:
“I am afraid it will not go with my dress,” she answered; “and, besides,
the Chamberlain’s nephew has sent me some real jewels, and everybody
knows that jewels cost far more than flowers.”

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote gives both reasons: the rose would not go with her dress, and the Chamberlain’s nephew had sent real jewels.

questions.question: What happened to the rose after the girl rejected it?
questions.expected: The Student threw it into the street, where it fell in the gutter and a cart-wheel went over it.

evidence.quote:
and he threw the rose into the street, where it fell into the gutter, and
a cart-wheel went over it.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote states that the Student threw the rose into the street, where it fell in the gutter and a cart-wheel went over it.

questions.question: What did the Giant recognize on the little boy’s hands and feet, and what explanation did the child give?
questions.expected: The Giant saw nail prints, which the child called the wounds of Love.

evidence.quote:
on the palms of the child’s hands were the prints of
two nails, and the prints of two nails were on the little feet.
“Nay!” answered the child; “but these are the wounds of Love.”

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes describe nail prints on the child’s hands and feet and the child’s explanation that they are the wounds of Love.

questions.question: What does the Miller take from Hans’s garden during the seasons when Hans is prosperous?
questions.expected: He plucks nosegays or herbs and takes plums and cherries when they are in season.

evidence.quote:
he would never go by his garden without leaning over
the wall and plucking a large nosegay, or a handful of sweet herbs, or
filling his pockets with plums and cherries if it was the fruit season.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote lists nosegays, sweet herbs, plums, and cherries as things the Miller takes.

questions.question: Why does the Miller say he will not let Hans visit his warm home in winter?
questions.expected: He claims Hans might envy their comforts, and says envy would spoil Hans’s nature.

evidence.quote:
he might get envious, and envy is
a most terrible thing, and would spoil anybody’s nature.

I certainly
will not allow Hans’ nature to be spoiled.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes say the Miller feared Hans might envy their comforts and claimed envy would spoil Hans’s nature.

questions.question: Why did the Miller ask Hans to fetch the Doctor?
questions.expected: The Miller’s son had fallen from a ladder and been hurt, and the Miller said the Doctor lived far away on a bad night.

evidence.quote:
I am in great trouble.  My little
boy has fallen off a ladder and hurt himself, and I am going for the
Doctor.  But he lives so far away, and it is such a bad night

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says the Miller’s boy fell from a ladder and was hurt, and that the Doctor lived far away on a bad night.

questions.question: What made the Rocket too wet to go off during the wedding fireworks?
questions.expected: He had been crying, and his tears had soaked the gunpowder.

evidence.quote: He was so damp with crying that he could not go off at all.

The best
thing in him was the gunpowder, and that was so wet with tears that it
was of no use.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state that the Rocket was damp from crying and that his gunpowder was too wet with tears to be of use.

questions.question: What does the Roman Candle say about romance after the Catherine Wheel says it is dead?
questions.expected: The Roman Candle says romance never dies and is like the moon, living for ever.

evidence.quote:
But the Catherine Wheel shook her head.  “Romance is dead, Romance is
dead, Romance is dead,” she murmured.

“Nonsense!” said the Roman Candle, “Romance never dies.  It is like the
moon, and lives for ever.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes identify the Catherine Wheel as saying romance is dead and the Roman Candle as saying it never dies and is like the moon.

questions.question: What does the clear crystal cup signify at the Prince and Princess’s banquet, and what happens if false lips touch it?
questions.expected: It signifies true love; false lips make it grow grey, dull, and cloudy.

evidence.quote:
Only true lovers could drink out of this cup, for if false lips
touched it, it grew grey and dull and cloudy.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote states that only true lovers could drink from the cup and that false lips made it grey, dull, and cloudy.

questions.question: What happens after the Swallow brings the Prince’s gold to the poor, and what happens after the children return to the Giant’s garden?
questions.expected: The poor children’s faces grow rosier and they laugh and play; in the Giant’s garden, the returning children are followed by the Spring.

evidence.quote:
Leaf after leaf of the fine gold he
brought to the poor, and the children’s faces grew rosier, and they
laughed and played games in the street.

And the other children, when they saw that the
Giant was not wicked any longer, came running back, and with them came
the Spring.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state that the poor children grew rosier, laughed, and played, and that the returning children came with the Spring.

questions.question: What does the Student say he will study?
questions.expected: He says he will go back to Philosophy and study Metaphysics.

evidence.quote:
as in this age to be practical is everything, I shall go back to
Philosophy and study Metaphysics.”

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says the Student will go back to Philosophy and study Metaphysics.

questions.question: What does the Miller say he has given Hans, and what does he say Hans is going to give him?
questions.expected: The Miller says he has given Hans his wheelbarrow, and that Hans is going to give him his plank.

evidence.quote:
I have given
you my wheelbarrow, and now you are going to give me your plank.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote directly says the Miller had given Hans his wheelbarrow and that Hans was going to give him the plank.

questions.question: What physical ability was Prince Dolor unable to develop after the christening accident?
questions.expected: He could not walk; his legs remained useless despite his otherwise sound body.

evidence.quote:
He could not walk, it is true; his limbs were mere useless appendages to
his body; but the body itself was strong and sound.

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote says Dolor could not walk, his limbs were useless, and his body was strong and sound.

questions.question: What does the little old woman say about her name and her connection to Prince Dolor?
questions.expected: She says she has many names, gave Dolor his name, and is his godmother.

evidence.quote: The little old woman laughed like a chime of silver bells.

“I have not got a name--or, rather, I have so many names that I don't
know which to choose. However, it was I who gave you yours, and you will
belong to me all your days. I am your godmother.”

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes identify her as the little old woman and state that she has many names, gave Dolor his name, and is his godmother.

questions.question: What did Dolor wish for before receiving the gold spectacles, and what did he wish for before receiving the silver ears?
questions.expected: He wished he could see better through glasses like his nurse’s; later he wished his godmother would give him a second pair of ears.

evidence.quote:
“I wonder,” he thought, “whether I could see better through a pair of
glasses like those my nurse reads with, and takes such care of. How I
would take care of them, too, if I only had a pair!”

“I wonder if my
godmother would give me a second pair of ears.”

evidenceReview.rationale: The quotes state both wishes: to see better through glasses like his nurse’s and for a second pair of ears from his godmother.

questions.question: Who tells Leander that the adder is dangerous, and what does the warning say?
questions.expected: A gardener warns him that they had tried to kill the adder because it was mischievous.

evidence.quote:
one
of the gardeners happened to come to the place where Leander was, and
spying the snake, cried out to his master: “Hold him fast, sir; it
is but an hour since we ran after him to kill him: it is the most
mischievous creature in the world.”

evidenceReview.rationale: The quote identifies a gardener and gives the warning that they had tried to kill the mischievous snake.

questions.question: What warning did Candide give Cherry about the ring, and what action immediately preceded its prick in this incident?
